records.sourceFile: The impact of test loads on the accuracy of 1RM prediction using the load-velocity relationship.pdf

paper.citation: Sayers MGL, Schlaeppi M, Hitz M, Lorenzetti S. The impact of test loads on the accuracy of 1RM prediction using the load-velocity relationship. BMC Sports Science, Medicine and Rehabilitation. 2018;10:9.
paper.abstract: Twelve recreational weight trainers had their Smith machine bench press 1RM measured, then performed bench press throws at 30 to 70% of 1RM with a linear position transducer. Regression models built from mean and peak bar velocity were compared, and the most accurate 1RM prediction came from peak velocity at 30, 40 and 50% of 1RM, with a fixed under-prediction of about 9 kg. The authors conclude that light-load bench press throws can predict 1RM without lifting near-maximal loads.
paper.tldr: A light-load bench press throw test using peak bar velocity at 30, 40 and 50% of 1RM predicted Smith machine 1RM in recreational lifters with high correlation. It under-predicted 1RM by about 9 kg, so it is best used as a rough starting estimate.
paper.methods: Methodological validation study in 12 recreational weight trainers. Smith machine 1RM was measured directly, then bench press throws were performed at 30, 40, 50, 60 and 70% of 1RM with a linear position transducer. Three-load regression models from the Jidovtseff approach were built with mean and peak velocity and compared with measured 1RM using ANOVA, Bland-Altman plots, CV% and ICC.
paper.findings: The peak velocity model using 30, 40 and 50% of 1RM gave the most accurate prediction (R2 = 0.96, SSE = 4.2 kg, ICC 0.967), but predicted values were about 9 kg below measured 1RM, and this difference was significant (P < 0.001). Mean velocity models had R2 of 0.85 to 0.89 and no significant mean difference from measured 1RM, though Bland-Altman plots showed accuracy problems. Slope and intercept values differed between mean and peak velocity models, but the abscissa (Load0) did not.
paper.limitations: Only 12 recreational lifters were tested, the velocity data came from a single session, and between-session reliability was not assessed. The test was done only on a Smith machine bench press with bench press throws, so results may not transfer to free-weight lifting or other exercises. The 1RM is extrapolated beyond the tested load range, which the authors note compromises accuracy, and the best model under-predicted 1RM.
paper.practicalImplications: Practitioners testing recreational lifters on a Smith machine could use three bench press throws at 30, 40 and 50% of an estimated 1RM, with peak bar velocity, to get a rough 1RM estimate and a training load reference. Because the model under-predicted by about 9 kg, the estimate should be treated as approximate.
paper.athleteDev: Light-load bench press throw testing could give a rough 1RM estimate for athletes new to lifting without near-maximal lifts. The study did not test whether the method tracks strength change over time, and its accuracy for youth or trained athletes is unknown.
paper.rtp: The study does not include injured athletes and does not address return to sport. It cannot be used to judge when an injured athlete has regained enough strength to return to play.

records.sourceFile: The influence of cuff width sex and race on arterial     occlusion - Implications for blood flow restriction research.pdf

paper.citation: Jessee MB, Buckner SL, Dankel SJ, Counts BR, Abe T, Loenneke JP. The Influence of Cuff Width, Sex, and Race on Arterial Occlusion: Implications for Blood Flow Restriction Research. Sports Medicine. 2016.
paper.abstract: The study examined upper arm arterial occlusion pressure (AOP) across three cuff widths (5, 10 and 12 cm) in 249 participants, and how individual characteristics, sex and race affect it. AOP was highest for the 5 cm cuff, and arm circumference and resting systolic pressure explained the most variance for each cuff. Men required greater pressures, and non-Hispanic Blacks required greater pressures than Whites after controlling for sex. Regression equations were created for each cuff width.
paper.tldr: Wider blood flow restriction cuffs need less pressure to stop arterial flow, and arm circumference and resting systolic pressure explain most of the individual variation. Report the cuff width and set restriction relative to each person's occlusion pressure; the equations were built on healthy adults, not athletes.
paper.methods: Participants had arm length, arm circumference and resting brachial blood pressure measured, then AOP was found in the standing position for each cuff with a Doppler probe at the radial artery, with 5 minutes of rest between cuffs applied in counterbalanced order. Repeated measures ANOVA compared cuff widths, hierarchical regression identified predictors, and a random 66% split was used to build and cross-validate equations.
paper.findings: AOP differed by cuff width (p<0.001), with 145 mmHg for the 5 cm cuff, 123 mmHg for 10 cm and 120 mmHg for 12 cm. The full model (arm circumference, systolic and diastolic pressure, arm length and sex) explained 56 to 65% of the variance. Men had higher AOP than women at each width, with small effects (d 0.33 to 0.46). Non-Hispanic Blacks (n=59) had higher AOP than Whites (n=173) at each width (for example 154 vs 142 mmHg at 5 cm), with d of 0.66 to 0.76, which the authors describe as relatively small for prescribing BFR.
paper.limitations: Participants were healthy adults aged 18 to 34, not athletes, and AOP was measured at rest in standing, not during exercise. Blood flow volume was not measured, only presence or absence of radial pulse. The racial comparison was a retrospective analysis limited to Black and White participants because of sample size.
paper.practicalImplications: Because cuff width changes the pressure needed to occlude flow, training studies and programs should report the cuff width used and set pressure relative to each person's occlusion pressure. The authors suggest the equations can estimate occlusion pressure for three common cuff widths, but they were derived for healthy non-athletes and should be checked before use with athletes.
paper.athleteDev: Cuff width changes the pressure needed to restrict arterial flow, so blood flow restriction training prescriptions for athletes should name the cuff and set pressure relative to the individual. The equations were built on non-athlete adults and have not been tested in trained performers.
paper.rtp: This study cannot inform return to sport. It measured occlusion pressure in healthy young adults at rest and did not assess injured athletes, rehabilitation outcomes or tissue response.

records.sourceFile: The predictive validity of a single leg bridge test for      hamstring injuries in Australian Rules Football     players.pdf

paper.citation: Freckleton G, Cook J, Pizzari T. The predictive validity of a single leg bridge test for hamstring injuries in Australian Rules Football players. Br J Sports Med. 2014;48:713-717.
paper.abstract: Preseason single leg hamstring bridge (SLHB) scores were measured in 482 amateur and semi-elite Australian Rules players and injuries were tracked through the 2011 season. Players who later had a right hamstring injury had lower right SLHB scores, and age, prior knee injury and prior hamstring injury were other associated factors. The authors conclude that low hamstring strength appears to be a risk factor, but confounding and a low injury rate limit interpretation.
paper.tldr: A simple preseason bridge test was lower in Australian football players who later strained their right hamstring, but the link did not hold once age and past injury were accounted for. Treat the SLHB as a screening idea, not a validated predictor.
paper.methods: Prospective cohort. Preseason SLHB repetitions and ankle dorsiflexion were measured in 482 players, and hamstring injuries were confirmed by a physiotherapist or doctor and tracked weekly through the 2011 season. Univariate tests were followed by logistic regression on variables with P below 1.0.
paper.findings: Twenty-eight hamstring injuries occurred (16 right, 12 left). Players with a right-side injury had a lower right SLHB (20.31 vs 25.98 reps, P = 0.029), were older, and were more likely to have a prior right hamstring or right knee injury. Left SLHB did not differ for left-side injuries. In the right-side logistic regression no factor was significant (right SLHB ratio 1.047, 95% CI 0.978 to 1.12, P = 0.190); in the left-side model, left leg dominance remained significant (ratio 8.66, 95% CI 2.60 to 28.83, P < 0.001).
paper.limitations: The 5.5% injury rate gave low power for regression. Age and prior injury confound the SLHB result, and not all players at each club were tested, which may bias the sample. Injuries were confirmed clinically rather than by imaging, and results come from one season. The Discussion says no significant factors were found in logistic regression, but Table 5 shows left leg dominance as significant for left-side injury; the table value is reported here. The authors note the SLHB may reflect an unrecovered prior strain rather than being a cause.
paper.practicalImplications: The SLHB is quick and needs no equipment, so it could serve as a screening step. The authors suggest testing whole elite squads in preseason to establish whether it adds value before it is used to flag players.
paper.athleteDev: The SLHB could be used in preseason screening to flag players for closer hamstring monitoring. This study does not show it predicts injury beyond age and injury history.
paper.rtp: The paper's clinical summary suggests the SLHB may help judge readiness to return to sport and track rehabilitation, but this cohort did not test either use. The study cannot establish a return-to-sport criterion.

records.sourceFile: The prognostic value of the hamstring outcome score to predict the risk of hamstring injuries.pdf

paper.citation: van de Hoef PA, Brink MS, van der Horst N, et al. The prognostic value of the hamstring outcome score to predict the risk of hamstring injuries. J Sci Med Sport. 2021.
paper.abstract: Cohort analysis of 356 amateur male soccer players from a cluster randomised trial. Lower HaOS scores were associated with more previous and new hamstring injuries. At an 80% HaOS cut-off, the modelled probability of a new injury was 11%, 18% and 28% for players with 0, 1 and 2 previous-season injuries. The HaOS may be useful when combined with injury history.
paper.tldr: A simple baseline symptom questionnaire, the HaOS, was lower in amateur soccer players who later had hamstring injuries, and risk rose with prior injuries. It flags risk modestly and is not a stand-alone screening test.
paper.methods: Prospective cohort derived from a 2016 to 2017 cluster-randomised trial of 400 adult male amateur players from 32 teams in the Netherlands. Baseline HaOS and previous injuries were recorded, and new injuries were reported weekly and verified by medical staff. Analyses used ANOVA, t-tests, univariable and bivariable logistic regression, restricted cubic splines and an interaction model, with multiple imputation for 44 missing HaOS totals.
paper.findings: Of 356 analysed players, 57 sustained a new injury. Injured players had lower total HaOS scores (77.1 vs 85.5, mean difference 8.5, 95% CI 3.8 to 13.2) and lower scores on every subscale. The HaOS-only model had an area under the ROC curve of 0.672, and adding the number of previous injuries raised it to 0.690 (likelihood ratio test P < 0.001). Previous injuries alone gave 0.643. At the 80% cut-off, modelled injury probability was 11%, 18% and 28% for 0, 1 and 2 previous injuries.
paper.limitations: HaOS was measured once at season start. Previous injuries were self-reported and recalled, and new injuries were not confirmed by imaging. Discrimination was modest and the model was not externally validated. This is a secondary analysis of trial participants, and the 44 missing HaOS totals were imputed under a missing-at-random assumption.
paper.practicalImplications: The HaOS can show which players report symptoms linked to higher hamstring risk, especially those with previous hamstring injuries. The authors still recommend that all players take part in hamstring prevention programmes, and say targeted prevention needs further studies and validated prediction models first.
paper.athleteDev: The HaOS combined with injury history can help staff talk with players about their hamstring risk. It should not be used to decide who skips prevention work, since neither a low score nor a previous injury identifies which players will actually be injured.
paper.rtp: This is a preseason study, not a return-to-play study. The study did not test the HaOS for return-to-play decisions and cannot support them.

records.sourceFile: The validity and reliability of wearable microtechnology for intermittent team sports - A systematic review.pdf

paper.citation: Crang ZL, Duthie G, Cole MH, Weakley J, Hewitt A, Johnston RD. The Validity and Reliability of Wearable Microtechnology for Intermittent Team Sports: A Systematic Review. Sports Medicine. 2020.
paper.abstract: This systematic review of 72 studies found that the validity and reliability of GNSS, local positioning and inertial wearable devices in team sports depend on the brand, sampling rate, movement type and intensity. Practitioners should consider device accuracy and repeatability when making training load decisions.
paper.tldr: Wearable GPS and tracking data are only as good as the specific device, sampling rate and movement being measured. Devices at 10 Hz or above were generally more accurate and reliable than 1 or 5 Hz units, and several metrics have been tested in only one or a few studies.
paper.methods: PRISMA systematic review (March 2020 search) of SPORTDiscus, CINAHL and MEDLINE for English-language peer-reviewed studies of validity and/or reliability of wearable microtechnology for intermittent team sport movement. Two authors screened records and extracted data; quality was scored on a modified Downs and Black checklist. Results were summarised narratively by metric, device and study type because of heterogeneity.
paper.findings: 72 studies were included: 384 records retrieved, 187 duplicates removed, 88 full texts assessed, 62 included plus 10 from reference lists. GNSS was generally valid for total distance in shuttle, continuous and team sport circuit movements, but 1 Hz and 5 Hz devices were less accurate for short straight-line and direction-change movements; GNSS was generally accurate for peak velocity in straight-line sprinting. Between-device reliability was better for 10 Hz and above, and 5 Hz devices showed poor reliability for accelerations above 3 m/s2. LPS was accurate for distance when set up correctly (bias 0.5 to 1.8%) but not with sub-optimal set-up (bias 15.0 to 29.5%), and its instantaneous velocity and acceleration errors rose with repeated change of direction. Intra-device reliability was poorly studied because identical movements cannot be repeated.
paper.limitations: Narrative synthesis only, with heterogeneous methods and devices. Many validity studies used timing gates, tape measures or radar rather than gold-standard 3D motion capture, and several metrics were based on a single device or system. Intra-device reliability values mix biological and technological variation. Only English-language journal articles from three databases were searched, and the search ended in March 2020.
paper.practicalImplications: Practitioners should check the sampling rate, set-up and movement type behind any device metric before using it for training load decisions. Devices at 10 Hz or above are the safer choice for distance and high-speed measures, and comparisons between players should use devices of the same type. The review does not provide thresholds for individual decisions.
paper.athleteDev: Training load tracking is only as reliable as the device and metric used, so performance staff should interpret speed, distance and acceleration data within the device error before prescribing top-up sessions or progressing training. The review does not test performance outcomes.
paper.rtp: The review covers device accuracy in healthy team sport movement and cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It does note that device error should be accounted for when rehabilitation loads are increased using speed and distance data.

records.sourceFile: To jog or to stride - A comparison between two standardised running tests to monitor neuromuscular status in team sport athletes.pdf

paper.citation: Leduc C, Sawczuk T, Russell S, Lacome M, Garrett JM. To jog or to stride: A comparison between two standardised running tests to monitor neuromuscular status in team sport athletes. Journal of Sports Sciences. 2024.
paper.abstract: This study compared two submaximal running tests, a 5-minute shuttle run (SRT-jog) and a repeated stride effort (SRT-stride), for monitoring neuromuscular fatigue after rugby union matches. Twenty-three male players were tested before a match and on the following two days. SRT-jog increased the day after the match, and SRT-stride increased on both days. Only SRT-stride changes were related to match locomotor variables, so the authors suggest it may be the more sensitive monitoring tool.
paper.tldr: In these university rugby players, both running tests changed the day after a match, but only the stride test stayed raised on day 2 and tracked match load. Staff who monitor post-match fatigue with a running test may prefer the stride protocol, but the evidence comes from one squad.
paper.methods: Longitudinal observational study run within routine practice from September 2019 to March 2020. Players wore GPS and accelerometer units in matches. Two days before, and one and two days after, each match they completed SRT-jog (5 minutes of 20 m shuttles at 9 km/h, scored on vertical accelerometer load) and SRT-stride (four 60 m runs at about 18 km/h, scored on a running load index). Linear mixed models with player and match location as random factors reported effect sizes with 90% confidence intervals.
paper.findings: SRT-jog increased on the day after the match (ES 0.63, 90% CI 0.37 to 0.89) and not on day 2 (ES 0.13). SRT-stride increased on day 1 (ES 0.24) and day 2 (ES 0.33). SRT-stride changes were associated with collisions (ES 0.58, 90% CI 0.18 to 0.99) and, with a CI crossing zero, total distance (ES 0.41). No match variables were associated with SRT-jog changes.
paper.limitations: Only 23 male players from one university squad, with no gold-standard fatigue measure, so the tests are judged on sensitivity. Players used their usual recovery strategies after the first test, which may have affected the day-2 results, and the authors suggest the SRT-jog speed may have limited its sensitivity. The abstract calls the total-distance association significant, but its 90% CI crosses zero (-0.01 to 0.83).
paper.practicalImplications: A stride-based submaximal run may be a practical way to track post-match neuromuscular status in running-based team sports. Standardise the running speed and protocol across the squad, since the authors link the shuttle test's weak results partly to speed choice.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: Use the stride-based test as a post-match neuromuscular check in running-based team sports, at the same speed each time, so that changes can be compared from session to session. The shuttle version responded on day 1 but was not linked to match load, so it adds less to interpretation here.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: Cannot inform return to sport. The players were injury-free for the prior six months and the study looks at normal post-match fatigue, not injury recovery or clearance decisions.

records.sourceFile: Towards Achilles Tendon Injury Prevention in Athletes with Structural MRI Biomarkers - A Machine Learning Approach.pdf

paper.citation: Kapinski N, Jaskulski K, Witkowska J, Kozlowski A, Adamczyk P, Wysoczanski B, et al. Towards Achilles Tendon Injury Prevention in Athletes with Structural MRI Biomarkers: A Machine Learning Approach. Sports Medicine - Open. 2024;10:118.
paper.abstract: 72 athletes had short-echo T2* gradient-echo MRI of both Achilles tendons, scored by a radiologist and by AI software, and were tested for dynamic strength, range of motion, muscle torque and balance. Structure-function correlations were modest (Spearman coefficients up to 0.49 for AI scoring), but structural features explained up to 59% of variance in functional groups with AI scoring, versus up to 20% with radiologist scoring. The authors conclude that AI-based scoring was superior and that the relationships are non-linear.
paper.tldr: In healthy sports participants, Achilles MRI features relate to strength, balance and range of motion, and AI-based scoring linked structure to function more strongly than radiologist scoring. This is a cross-sectional association study, so it does not show that the scores predict Achilles injury.
paper.methods: Cross-sectional study of 72 participants without Achilles injury history. Both tendons were scanned with a short-echo T2* gradient-echo sequence on 3T and 1.5T scanners and scored on six structural parameters by a radiologist and by SmarterOrthoMRI software. Functional tests were jumps on a force plate, single-leg balance, goniometer range of motion and muscle torque, reduced by principal component analysis. Relationships were tested with Spearman correlation and normalised mutual information, and models (decision trees, random forests, AutoGluon) were trained with 10-fold cross-validation.
paper.findings: AI-based structural scores gave higher maximal Spearman coefficients than radiologist scores in three of four functional groups (for example 0.49 vs 0.36 for range of motion), with balance the exception (0.33 vs 0.35). Table 3 counts more significant structure-function relationships with AI scoring in all four groups (for example 31 vs 29 for dynamic strength and 12 vs 9 for muscle torque), although the text says the torque count favored radiologists. Structural features explained 33 to 59% of functional variance with AI inputs and 6 to 20% with radiologist inputs.
paper.limitations: A small cross-sectional sample with exploratory analyses; the best models were chosen using fit on the test folds and the whole dataset, so explained variance is likely optimistic, and 28 participants lacked balance data. The software belongs to the authors' company, which also funded the study, and the text's torque count conflicts with Table 3.
paper.practicalImplications: Achilles MRI structure may help explain differences in strength, balance and mobility, and a short T2* protocol could be a candidate for screening studies. Do not use these scores to predict injury or make return-to-sport decisions until prospective studies support it.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: The findings link Achilles structure to strength, balance and range of motion in sports participants, which could guide future monitoring work. The study does not show that changing training according to the MRI scores improves performance or reduces injury.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: Limited. The participants were uninjured, so the study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions; prospective work in injured athletes would be needed before the scores are used for clearance.

records.sourceFile: Tracking devices and physical performance analysis in team sports - A comprehensive framework for research, trends and future directions.pdf

paper.citation: Ferraz A, Duarte-Mendes P, Sarmento H, Valente-Dos-Santos J, Travassos B. Tracking devices and physical performance analysis in team sports: a comprehensive framework for research, trends and future directions. Frontiers in Sports and Active Living. 2023;5:1284086.
paper.abstract: This PRISMA-guided scoping review examined how GPS and local positioning tracking systems have been used in team-sport performance analysis from 2011 to 2023. Across 79 studies, tracking technology was used for match performance analysis, comparisons of training and match load, injury, and nutrition. Most work used kinematic and mechanical external-load metrics, with fewer studies integrating internal load. The authors propose a framework linking research strategies, metrics and applied decisions.
paper.tldr: Tracking data are used mostly to describe match and training demands, with fewer studies predicting injury or fatigue and very few on nutrition. The authors call for a framework that links external and internal load, and for more experimental work.
paper.methods: PRISMA-guided scoping review, registered with INPLASY, of PubMed, Web of Science and Scopus for English-language studies from January 2011 to July 2023 on GPS or local positioning systems with elite team-sport athletes. From 772 initial records, 79 studies were included after title and abstract screening and full-text review by two reviewers, with a third resolving disagreements. Quality was scored with a 16-item appraisal adapted from Faber et al. and Law et al.
paper.findings: Studies came mainly from football (41.8%), futsal (15.2%) and rugby (11.4%). By analysis type, characterization and comparison of drills, training and matches was the largest group (62.0%), followed by correlational studies (26.6%), studies predicting performance, fatigue or injury (8.7%) and experimental studies (2.7%). Mean study quality was 89.2%.
paper.limitations: Only English-language papers from three databases were included, and systematic reviews were excluded, so some relevant work may be missing. Reliability and validation studies were excluded, so the review does not judge device or metric validity, and quality scoring showed only moderate agreement (kappa 0.43).
paper.practicalImplications: Teams should choose tracking metrics to fit the question and, where possible, track external and internal load together. On injury, the authors cite work that the acute:chronic workload ratio predicts injury better than total workload, but they report conflicting findings across the screened studies and note that no injury forecast yet links match-demand scenarios to load.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: Use tracking data to compare training and match demands by position and session type, and check that the chosen metrics answer the coaching question. The review finds few studies on how training manipulations change match performance, so new drill designs should be trialled rather than assumed to work.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: Limited. The review covers healthy team-sport athletes and in-season injury studies; it does not evaluate rehabilitation or return-to-play criteria, so tracking data should not be used to clear players on this basis.

records.sourceFile: Tracking systems in team sports - A narrative review of applications of the data and sport specific analysis.pdf

paper.citation: Torres-Ronda L, Beanland E, Whitehead S, Sweeting A, Clubb J. Tracking Systems in Team Sports: A Narrative Review of Applications of the Data and Sport Specific Analysis. Sports Med Open. 2022;8:15.
paper.abstract: This narrative review summarises and critically evaluates tracking systems used in team sports and their applications for describing, planning and monitoring training and competition. It also discusses metric selection, time-analysis approaches and sport-specific considerations for seven popular team sports.
paper.tldr: Tracking data are useful for describing, planning and monitoring external load, but the choice of system, metric and time window must fit the sport and position. Practitioners should check the validity, reliability and ecological validity of any metric before relying on it.
paper.methods: Narrative review with no described literature search or selection process. The authors outline tracking technologies (GPS, optical, local positioning, IMU), metric categories, time-analysis methods, and sport-specific considerations for seven team sports.
paper.findings: The review presents tracking data as serving three overlapping purposes: describing, planning and monitoring external load. It notes that absolute values, peak demands from moving averages, and time series segmentation each suit different questions, and that optical tracking and GPS show slight-to-moderate differences for total distance but moderate-to-large differences for high-speed running. Sport-specific constraints such as field size, indoor play and competition rules determine which systems and metrics are usable.
paper.limitations: No systematic search or quality appraisal is described, so the evidence base is not transparent. Several sport-specific statements are drawn from unpublished observations and data. The authors note that many metrics and thresholds lack validation in specific sports, such as basketball and women's soccer.
paper.practicalImplications: Choose tracking metrics for the sport, position and training goal rather than defaulting to total distance or speed zones. Check how each manufacturer defines and filters metrics before comparing data across systems, and use peak-demand or time-series approaches where the training question needs them.
paper.athleteDev: Performance staff can use the review's framework to decide which tracking metrics and time windows fit a given sport, position and planning question, and to align tracking data with tactical and video context. The review gives no effect sizes, so the choices should be checked against each team's own data.
paper.rtp: The review does not evaluate return-to-sport decisions. It mentions rehabilitation planning only in general terms, so it cannot be used to set return-to-play criteria.

records.sourceFile: Training load and acute performance decrements following different training sessions.pdf

paper.citation: Vermeire KM, Caen K, Bourgois JG, Boone J. Training Load and Acute Performance Decrements Following Different Training Sessions. Int J Sports Physiol Perform. 2023 (ahead of print).
paper.abstract: Eleven recreational male cyclists completed four training sessions of different intensity and duration, each followed by a 3-km time trial. Training load metrics gave different rankings of the sessions, and only the rating-of-perceived-exertion load followed the acute performance decrement in the study.
paper.tldr: Different training load methods rank the same sessions differently, so a method chosen for one session type may misjudge another. Session RPE-based load best matched the performance drop after a short interval session in this study.
paper.methods: Eleven recreationally active men completed a step incremental test, two baseline 3-km time trials, and then four randomised training sessions (short-duration intervals, long-duration intervals, medium-intensity, and low-intensity), each followed by a 3-km time trial. Seven load metrics were calculated from heart rate, power and RPE, and time-trial power was expressed relative to baseline. Repeated-measures ANOVA and Cohen d were used.
paper.findings: Only the short-duration interval session reduced time-trial power (5.3% [3.9%], P = .003, large effect size of 1.26); time trials after the other three sessions were better than after the short interval session but did not differ from baseline or from each other. Session RPE-based load, individualised TRIMP and Training Stress Score ranked the short interval session highest, while total work done ranked the low-intensity session highest. Banister, Edwards and Lucia heart-rate TRIMPs did not separate the short interval session from the medium- and low-intensity sessions.
paper.limitations: The sample was small (n = 11), the sessions were indoors and fixed in structure, and only one time-trial outcome was used. The authors note that the acute-decrement approach is not a gold standard, and the abstract says only RPE-based load matched the decrement, while the conclusion names RPE-based load, individualised TRIMP and TSS. The abstract describes 7 load metrics while the methods list 8 (including the power-based Lucia TRIMP used to equate sessions), and Table 2 gives the same mean power (336.6 W) for two sessions, which may be a typographical error.
paper.practicalImplications: Different training load methods can rank the same sessions differently even with the same input, so coaches should choose and state the method used. Total work done should not be used to match or compare sessions, and session RPE captured the effect of the most intense session on performance in this study.
paper.athleteDev: When planning cycling sessions, check which load method is used before comparing sessions, since duration-weighted metrics can undervalue short hard intervals. Session RPE can be used as a practical check on intensity, though this small indoor study does not show that it is the best measure for every athlete or sport.
paper.rtp: This study cannot inform return to sport. It tested recreational cyclists doing training sessions and did not study injured athletes or rehabilitation.

records.sourceFile: Training load monitoring in team sports - A practical approach to addressing missing data.pdf

paper.citation: Griffin A, Kenny IC, Comyns TM, Purtill H, Tiernan C, O'Shaughnessy E, et al. Training load monitoring in team sports: a practical approach to addressing missing data. Journal of Sports Sciences. 2021.
paper.abstract: Examines the effect of missing session-RPE training load data on load metrics in professional soccer, and compares 12 missing value imputation methods across 5% to 50% missingness.
paper.tldr: Missing session-RPE data distort ACWR, monotony and strain, so fill gaps before calculating them. The daily team mean gave the most accurate values across missingness levels.
paper.methods: Secondary analysis of season-long daily session-RPE from 10 male professional soccer players, with data removed at random in 5% steps. Twelve imputation methods were scored by normalised root-mean-square error and mean absolute deviation.
paper.findings: Daily Team Mean gave the lowest NRMSE (0.42 to 0.46) at all missingness levels, and at 10% missingness it had NRMSE 0.43 against 0.56 for Player Mean; in Table 3 Daily Team Median had slightly lower mean absolute deviation (6.8 to 70.6 vs 7.3 to 72.1). Mean absolute deviation rose with missingness for every method. The figures show that unaddressed missing values can distort ACWR, monotony and strain, and the study reports no statistical tests of these effects.
paper.limitations: Only 10 players from one club were studied, and missing data were simulated as completely at random. The team-mean method does not apply outside team settings, and the effects on the load metrics are shown graphically for one player rather than tested statistically. The discussion swaps the MAD ranges for Daily Team Mean and Median relative to Table 3; the table values are reported here.
paper.practicalImplications: Keep missing session-RPE data to a minimum. Where a gap is unavoidable, fill it with the daily team mean before calculating ACWR, monotony or strain, and review monitoring practice if missingness exceeds about 10%.
paper.athleteDev: Fill missing session-RPE values with the daily team mean before calculating load metrics, and aim for a complete record on every training day. Treat imputed values with caution on match days or where players' session durations differ, as the paper's example shows.
paper.rtp: The method is designed for team training loads, and the paper notes it does not apply to a player in rehabilitation who is away from team activities. It cannot be used to set return-to-play loads for those players.
